solution:
The **light reaction** (photochemical reaction) takes place in the **thylakoid membranes** of the grana. Its steps are:

1. **Absorption of light:** chlorophylls, carotenes and xanthophylls in the thylakoid membranes absorb light. The accessory pigments and other chlorophyll molecules act as **antenna molecules** and pass the energy to the **reaction centres**, \(\text{P}_{680}\) of **PS-II** and \(\text{P}_{700}\) of **PS-I**.
2. **Excitation of chlorophyll:** a photon boosts an electron of the reaction-centre chlorophyll to a higher energy level. The excited chlorophyll gives out the electron and is oxidized.
3. **Photolysis of water:** the oxidized \(\text{P}_{680}\) regains electrons by splitting water: \(4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4\text{e}^-\). Oxygen is given out as a byproduct.
4. **Electron transport:** the electrons emitted by PS-II pass through a chain of electron carriers and are trapped by \(\text{P}_{700}\) of PS-I.
5. **Photophosphorylation:** protons accumulate inside the thylakoid and form a **proton gradient**. The energy released when the protons diffuse across the thylakoid membrane into the stroma is used to form **ATP** from ADP.
6. **Formation of \(\text{NADPH}_2\):** electrons emitted by excited PS-I flow down a chain of carriers to \(\text{NADP}^+\), which takes up the protons from water and is reduced to \(\text{NADPH}_2\), the **reducing power** of the cell.
7. In **cyclic photophosphorylation**, electrons from PS-I return to PS-I itself and only ATP is formed; in **non-cyclic photophosphorylation** both ATP and \(\text{NADPH}_2\) are formed and oxygen is evolved.

**Link with the dark reaction:** ATP and \(\text{NADPH}_2\) (the assimilatory power) produced in the thylakoids move into the **stroma**, where the dark reaction (Calvin cycle) uses them. ATP and \(\text{NADPH}_2\) reduce 3-PGA to 3-PGAL, and ATP is also spent in regenerating RuBP; in all, 18 ATP and 12 \(\text{NADPH}_2\) are used to fix 6 \(\text{CO}_2\) into one glucose molecule. In turn the Calvin cycle returns ADP and \(\text{NADP}^+\) to the light reaction, so the two reactions run one after the other.

[Note: the textbook says the protons diffuse into the stroma "against" the \(\text{H}^+\) concentration gradient; they actually move down the gradient, from the high concentration inside the thylakoid to the lower concentration in the stroma.]

**a. Respiration and photorespiration**

| Point | Respiration | Photorespiration |
|---|---|---|
| When it occurs | All the time, in light and in dark | In light, under high temperature, bright light, high \(\text{O}_2\) and low \(\text{CO}_2\) |
| Where it occurs | In all living cells, in the cytoplasm and mitochondria | In green cells of \(\text{C}_3\) plants, involving chloroplast, peroxisomes and mitochondria |
| Substrate | Glucose (carbohydrate) | RuBP, which RuBisCO oxygenates to PGA and phosphoglycolate |
| Outcome | Food is oxidized and energy is released as ATP for life processes | Wasteful: \(\text{CO}_2\) is given out instead of being fixed, and about 25% of the photosynthetically fixed carbon is lost |

**b. Absorption spectrum and action spectrum**

| Point | Absorption spectrum | Action spectrum |
|---|---|---|
| What the graph shows | Light absorbed at different wavelengths by different pigments | Rate of photosynthesis at different wavelengths of light |
| What is measured | Absorption of light by each pigment (chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, carotenoids) | Photosynthetic activity of the plant |
| What it tells us | Which wavelengths each pigment absorbs: chlorophyll a and b absorb most in the blue, violet and red | Which wavelengths drive photosynthesis: mainly red and blue |
| Example in the chapter | Graph 12.3 | Graph 12.4 |

The two spectra for chlorophyll a and b overlap and coincide, which shows that the light absorbed by chlorophyll is the light used in photosynthesis.

**c. Cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation**

| Point | Cyclic photophosphorylation | Non-cyclic photophosphorylation |
|---|---|---|
| Photosystems involved | PS-I only | Both PS-I and PS-II |
| Path of electrons | Electrons leave the reaction centre of PS-I and return to it | Electrons released from PS-II do not return to it; they pass through an electron transport chain to PS-I and then reduce \(\text{NADP}^+\) |
| Photolysis of water | Does not occur, so no oxygen is evolved | Occurs, and oxygen is evolved |
| Products | ATP only | ATP and \(\text{NADPH}_2\) (assimilatory power) |

[Note: the chapter does not describe ordinary respiration (it is treated in the chapter on respiration); the respiration column of table (a) rests on that general knowledge, not on this chapter.]

The **light reaction** is common to both: in \(\text{C}_3\) and \(\text{C}_4\) plants light is trapped by chlorophyll, water undergoes photolysis, oxygen is evolved, and ATP and \(\text{NADPH}_2\) are formed. The **Calvin cycle (\(\text{C}_3\) pathway)** is also common to both, with its three steps: **carboxylation** of RuBP by RuBisCO to form 3-PGA, **glycolytic reversal** in which 3-PGA is reduced to 3-PGAL using ATP and \(\text{NADPH}_2\), and **regeneration of RuBP**. In \(\text{C}_3\) plants the Calvin cycle runs in the mesophyll cells, while in \(\text{C}_4\) plants it runs in the chloroplasts of the bundle sheath cells, on the \(\text{CO}_2\) released from malic acid. The extra step found only in \(\text{C}_4\) plants is the first fixation of \(\text{CO}_2\) by PEP in the mesophyll cells to form oxaloacetic acid.

They are located **outside the thylakoids, in the stroma** of the chloroplast. Carbon fixation occurs in the stroma by a series of enzyme-catalysed steps, and the ATP and \(\text{NADPH}_2\) produced in the thylakoids during the light reaction come into the stroma, where carbohydrates are synthesized. The thylakoid membranes carry the pigments and photosystems of the light reaction.

The three phases of the Calvin cycle (\(\text{C}_3\) pathway) are **carboxylation**, **glycolytic reversal (reduction)** and **regeneration of RuBP**.

1. **Carboxylation:** the 5-carbon sugar **ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP)** reacts with \(\text{CO}_2\) in the presence of **RuBP carboxylase (RuBisCO)** to give an unstable 6-carbon intermediate, which at once splits into two molecules of **3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA)**. *Significance:* this is the step in which atmospheric \(\text{CO}_2\) is fixed into an organic compound; because its first stable product has 3 carbons, the pathway is called the \(\text{C}_3\) pathway.
2. **Glycolytic reversal:** 3-PGA uses ATP to form 1,3-diphosphoglyceric acid, which is reduced to **glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (3-PGAL)** by \(\text{NADPH}_2\) supplied by the light reaction. *Significance:* here the ATP and \(\text{NADPH}_2\) of the light reaction are used, so the energy trapped from sunlight is stored in the sugar; of every 12 molecules of 3-PGAL, 2 are used to make one glucose molecule.
3. **Regeneration of RuBP:** the remaining 10 molecules of 3-PGAL are used, through a series of reactions and at the cost of 6 ATP, to regenerate 6 molecules of RuBP. *Significance:* the cycle can run continuously only if there is enough RuBP to accept fresh \(\text{CO}_2\); these reactions also give the plant a variety of organic compounds needed for its structure and function.

Six turns of the cycle are needed to make one glucose molecule, and the cycle returns ADP and \(\text{NADP}^+\) to the light reaction.

These are the **\(\text{C}_4\) plants**, which need 30 ATP per glucose molecule instead of 18, because regenerating PEP from pyruvic acid forms AMP and costs 12 additional ATP. Tropical regions have high temperature and bright light, the very conditions under which **photorespiration** occurs in \(\text{C}_3\) plants, when RuBisCO acts as an oxygenase and about 25% of the fixed carbon is lost. In \(\text{C}_4\) plants, \(\text{CO}_2\) is first fixed by PEP in the mesophyll cells and then released inside the bundle sheath cells, so the \(\text{CO}_2\) concentration there stays high and RuBisCO carries out carboxylation, not photorespiration. They can also fix \(\text{CO}_2\) even when its concentration in the air is very low, so the extra ATP spent is repaid by much higher productivity in hot, bright climates.

A photocentre (reaction centre, \(\text{P}_{680}\) or \(\text{P}_{700}\)) is surrounded by a cluster of chlorophyll and accessory pigment molecules, the **light harvesting** or **antenna molecules**. Different pigments absorb light of different wavelengths: chlorophyll a and b absorb mainly in the blue, violet and red, while carotenoids absorb in the violet to blue region. So a photon absorbed anywhere in the harvesting zone, at many different wavelengths, can pass its energy at a very high rate to the reaction centre, and much more of the light falling on the leaf is used. Carotenoids also protect the chlorophyll molecules from **photo-oxidation**.

The question has the two colours reversed: a chlorophyll solution appears **green in transmitted light** and **red in reflected light**.

**Green in transmitted light:** chlorophyll a and b absorb mostly the blue, violet and red wavelengths (absorption spectrum). The green part of the light is hardly absorbed, so it passes through the solution and the solution looks green.

**Red in reflected light:** when the chlorophyll extract is seen in a dark room by a flash of torch light (Activity 1), it appears red. The absorbed light excites the chlorophyll molecules, and as the excited molecules return to the ground state the energy comes out as red light.

**Significance for photosynthesis:** the green colour shows that green light is not absorbed and so is little used; the action spectrum confirms that photosynthesis is driven mainly by the red and blue light that chlorophyll absorbs. The red glow shows that chlorophyll is excited by the light it absorbs; in the leaf this excitation energy is passed to the reaction centres and used in the light reaction instead of being given out.

[Note: the textbook question says "green in reflected light and red in transmitted light", which is the wrong way round; the chapter's own box says red in reflected light and green in transmitted light. The chapter also does not name the phenomenon (fluorescence) or state that the excited chlorophyll gives out its energy as red light.]

Photosynthesis is the only process on earth by which **solar energy is trapped** by green plants and converted into food, so it is the final light-energy trapping process on which **all life ultimately depends**. This anabolic process uses inorganic substances (\(\text{CO}_2\) and water) and produces food for all living organisms, directly or indirectly. It transforms solar energy into **chemical energy**, and about 70 billion tons of carbon are fixed by green plants every year, making it one of the most massive chemical processes on earth. The oxygen released as a byproduct is needed for **aerobic respiration** of living organisms and also forms the protective **ozone layer** around the earth. Photosynthesis in the past has also given us **fossil fuels** such as coal, petroleum and natural gas.

In **non-cyclic photophosphorylation**, the high energy electrons released from PS-II (\(\text{P}_{680}\)) do not return to PS-II; they pass through the electron transport chain to PS-I and are finally used to reduce \(\text{NADP}^+\). The electron-deficient PS-II must regain its electrons, and it does so by oxidizing water: photolysis releases electrons, protons and oxygen. The electrons refill PS-II, the protons are accepted by \(\text{NADP}^+\) to form \(\text{NADPH}_2\), and oxygen is given out. In cyclic photophosphorylation the electrons return to PS-I itself, so no water needs to be split and no oxygen is evolved.

In \(\text{C}_4\) plants the chloroplasts of the **bundle sheath cells** contain the enzymes of the **Calvin cycle**, while the mesophyll cells first fix \(\text{CO}_2\) with PEP to form oxaloacetic acid and then malic acid. Malic acid is carried into the bundle sheath cells, where it releases \(\text{CO}_2\), so the concentration of \(\text{CO}_2\) becomes high there. At this high \(\text{CO}_2\) concentration RuBisCO works as a carboxylase in the Calvin cycle and not as an oxygenase, so photorespiration is avoided. The bundle sheath cells also surround the vascular bundles, so the sugar formed is transported easily into the phloem.

[Note: the chapter does not state directly that the mesophyll cells of \(\text{C}_4\) plants lack RuBisCO.]

Without **Kranz anatomy** there would be no separate bundle sheath around the vascular bundles in which \(\text{CO}_2\) released from malic acid could be concentrated around the Calvin cycle enzymes. RuBisCO would then work at the ordinary low \(\text{CO}_2\) concentration of the air, and under high temperature, bright light and high oxygen it would act as an oxygenase, so **photorespiration** would occur and about 25% of the fixed carbon would be lost. The plants would behave like \(\text{C}_3\) plants, losing their advantage of being better photosynthesizers, and the 12 extra ATP spent on the \(\text{C}_4\) pathway would be wasted.

RuBisCO acts as an oxygenase only when the oxygen concentration is high and the \(\text{CO}_2\) concentration is low. In \(\text{C}_4\) plants, \(\text{CO}_2\) is first fixed in the mesophyll cells as oxaloacetic acid and malic acid, and the malic acid releases its \(\text{CO}_2\) inside the bundle sheath cells, where RuBisCO is located. The \(\text{CO}_2\) concentration around RuBisCO therefore stays high, so it combines RuBP with \(\text{CO}_2\) (carboxylation) in the Calvin cycle and not with \(\text{O}_2\), and photorespiration does not take place.

**Accessory pigments** (chlorophyll b, carotenes and xanthophylls) act as light-harvesting antenna molecules that absorb light and pass the energy to the reaction centres; carotenoids absorb in the violet to blue region and transfer the energy to chlorophyll a. Without them, only the light absorbed by chlorophyll a itself could be used, so a much smaller part of the light falling on the leaf would be trapped and the rate of photosynthesis would fall. Carotenoids also protect chlorophyll from **photo-oxidation**, so without them chlorophyll molecules would be damaged in strong light.

1. **Leaf anatomy:** a section of a \(\text{C}_4\) leaf shows **Kranz anatomy**: a bundle sheath around the vascular bundles whose cells have large chloroplasts with almost no or poorly developed grana, while the mesophyll cells have small chloroplasts with well-developed grana. A \(\text{C}_3\) leaf does not show this arrangement.
2. **First stable product of \(\text{CO}_2\) fixation:** using the radioactive tracer technique with \(^{14}\text{CO}_2\), the first stable product can be identified. In \(\text{C}_3\) plants it is the 3-carbon compound **3-phosphoglyceric acid**, formed by the Calvin cycle; in \(\text{C}_4\) plants it is the 4-carbon compound **oxaloacetic acid**, formed from PEP.
3. **Photorespiration:** \(\text{C}_3\) plants show photorespiration under high temperature and bright light, while \(\text{C}_4\) plants do not.

These features justify the identification because the anatomy and the first product are what define the two pathways.

The few bundle sheath cells are supplied with \(\text{CO}_2\) by the many mesophyll cells around them. The mesophyll cells fix atmospheric \(\text{CO}_2\) with PEP to form oxaloacetic acid and then malic acid, which is sent into the bundle sheath cells and releases \(\text{CO}_2\) there, so the \(\text{CO}_2\) concentration in them becomes high. RuBisCO therefore works only as a carboxylase in the Calvin cycle and there is no photorespiration, so none of the fixed carbon is lost, unlike the 25% loss in \(\text{C}_3\) plants. \(\text{C}_4\) plants can also fix \(\text{CO}_2\) even when its concentration in the air is very low, so a small number of bundle sheath cells works very efficiently and the plants are highly productive.

In **Kranz anatomy** the vascular bundles of the leaf are surrounded by a bundle sheath, with two kinds of chloroplasts: small ones with well-developed grana in the mesophyll cells and large ones with poorly developed grana in the bundle sheath cells. This allows a **division of labour**: the mesophyll cells fix atmospheric \(\text{CO}_2\) with PEP (enzyme PEPCO) into oxaloacetic acid and malic acid, and the bundle sheath cells, which contain the Calvin cycle enzymes, receive the malic acid and release \(\text{CO}_2\) from it. The \(\text{CO}_2\) concentration in the bundle sheath therefore becomes high, so RuBisCO carries out carboxylation and photorespiration is prevented. Because the bundle sheath lies around the vascular bundles, the sugar formed in the Calvin cycle is passed easily into the phloem. As a result \(\text{C}_4\) plants are better photosynthesizers and can fix \(\text{CO}_2\) even at very low concentration.

The pathway is the **\(\text{C}_4\) pathway**, also called the **Hatch-Slack pathway**. The corrections are:

1. Atmospheric \(\text{CO}_2\) enters the **mesophyll cell**, not the bundle sheath cell.
2. **OAA is formed in the mesophyll cell:** PEP accepts \(\text{CO}_2\) with the help of PEP carboxylase (PEPCO), giving oxaloacetic acid.
3. OAA is converted to **malic acid** in the mesophyll cell, and malic acid is carried into the bundle sheath cell.
4. In the bundle sheath cell, malic acid gives **pyruvic acid** and releases \(\text{CO}_2\), which enters the \(\text{C}_3\) pathway (Calvin cycle).
5. It is **pyruvic acid**, not malic acid, that returns to the mesophyll cell, where it regenerates PEP by using one ATP (forming AMP).

Corrected pathway:

| Mesophyll cell | Bundle sheath cell |
|---|---|
| Atmospheric \(\text{CO}_2\) + PEP gives OAA (PEP carboxylase) | |
| OAA gives malic acid, which moves to the bundle sheath cell | Malic acid gives pyruvic acid + \(\text{CO}_2\) |
| | \(\text{CO}_2\) enters the \(\text{C}_3\) pathway (Calvin cycle) and forms sugar |
| Pyruvic acid + ATP regenerates PEP | Pyruvic acid returns to the mesophyll cell |

**Yes, the scheme is wrong:** the positions of **PS-I and PS-II are interchanged**. In non-cyclic photophosphorylation the electron flow starts at PS-II and ends at \(\text{NADP}^+\) through PS-I, and the electrons from water go to PS-II, not to PS-I.

Corrected scheme (non-cyclic photophosphorylation):

1. Light falls on **PS-II (\(\text{P}_{680}\))**, placed on the left. Its excited electrons go **up** to its primary acceptor, so the arrow runs from PS-II to the primary acceptor.
2. From this primary acceptor the electrons pass through the **cytochrome complex**, and ADP is converted to **ATP**.
3. The electrons then reach **PS-I (\(\text{P}_{700}\))**, placed on the right, which also absorbs light. Its excited electrons go up to its primary acceptor and on to **NADP reductase**.
4. NADP reductase reduces \(\text{NADP}^+\) to **NADPH** using the \(2\text{H}^+\) from water.
5. Photolysis of water, \(\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{H}^+ + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2 + 2\text{e}^-\), supplies the **2 electrons to PS-II** to replace those it lost; oxygen is released.

So the corrected order of electron flow is: water, PS-II, primary acceptor, cytochrome complex (ATP formed), PS-I, primary acceptor, NADP reductase, \(\text{NADP}^+\) (NADPH formed).
